# Conclusion {#sec-tumour-size}


::: {.callout-important title="Conclusion: we need to measure the glandular, less fatty tissue"}
The information is in the glandular/fibrous tissue, not in the fat. Fatty scans look almost the same in every cohort (@fig-cohort-parts),
while the water-rich scans show the water rising from NORMAL to BENIGN to CANCER, as the synchrotron and Keele ex-vivo data do
(@sec-by-cohort, @fig-synchrotron, @fig-keele). Comparing a patient's two breasts using only scans that reach glandular tissue, the CANCER
breast has the higher Water:Fat in **15/18 \(83%\)** of CANCER/NORMAL patients; using only the fatty
scans, it is **11/23 \(48%\)**, about chance. A measurement therefore has to be made in the
glandular, less fatty part of the breast. As the tumour sizes below show, it does not have to hit the tumour itself. @sec-on-the-fly proposes
one way of doing this during scanning, and @sec-mapping another: mapping the breast and choosing the regions after the scan. **We think
mapping is the way to go.**
:::

The size of each tumour in our CANCER breasts, by grade, measured two ways. From the pathology reports, the **linear extent** of invasive tumour
measured in the biopsy cores (the largest of a breast's specimens, lymph node specimens left out); from the radiology reports, the **largest mass
measured on imaging** (mammogram, ultrasound or MRI). The grade is the **overall (Nottingham) grade** from the pathology reports, taken from the
score out of 9 where the report gives one (3-5 grade 1, 6-7 grade 2, 8-9 grade 3) and from the stated grade otherwise. CANCER breasts with at
least one usable scan (@sec-on-the-fly) are highlighted.


::: {#cell-fig-tumour-size .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
GRADES = (1, 2, 3)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)  # the same horizontal jitter on every render

def plot_by_grade(ax, values, ylabel, title):
    by_grade = {g: [size for grade, size, _ in values if grade == g] for g in GRADES}
    ax.boxplot([by_grade[g] for g in GRADES], positions=range(len(GRADES)), widths=0.5, showfliers=False, patch_artist=True,
               boxprops=dict(facecolor="#d4ebe8", edgecolor="#2a9d8f"), whiskerprops=dict(color="#2a9d8f"), capprops=dict(color="#2a9d8f"),
               medianprops=dict(color="#1d3557", lw=2.2))
    for k, g in enumerate(GRADES):
        for is_usable in (False, True):
            here = [size for grade, size, ok in values if grade == g and ok == is_usable]
            ax.scatter(k + rng.uniform(-0.18, 0.18, len(here)), here, s=14 if is_usable else 10, zorder=3,
                       color=TOP_COLOUR if is_usable else "grey", alpha=0.9 if is_usable else 0.5,
                       edgecolor="black" if is_usable else "none", lw=0.4,
                       label=("usable scan" if is_usable else "no usable scan") if k == 0 else None)
    labels = []
    for g in GRADES:
        here = [(size, ok) for grade, size, ok in values if grade == g]
        labels.append(f"Grade {g}\nn={len(here)}\nmean {np.mean([s for s, _ in here]):.1f} mm\n{sum(ok for _, ok in here)} usable"
                      if here else f"Grade {g}\n(n=0)")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(GRADES)), labels)
    ax.set(ylabel=ylabel, title=title, ylim=(0, None))
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3, axis="y")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")

plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 7
fig, (biopsy_ax, imaging_ax) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.8))
plot_by_grade(biopsy_ax, tumours, "Linear extent (mm)", "Biopsy cores")
plot_by_grade(imaging_ax, imaged, "Largest mass on imaging (mm)", "Imaging")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 10

usable_sizes = [size for _, size, ok in tumours if ok]
other_sizes = [size for _, size, ok in tumours if not ok]
```

Boxes span the middle half of the breasts, the thick line is the median, and the whiskers reach the furthest breast within 1.5 box-lengths. Breasts with at least one usable scan are blue, the others grey.](tumour_size_files/figure-html/fig-tumour-size-output-1.png){#fig-tumour-size width=767 height=366}

:::


60 CANCER breasts have both a biopsy size and a grade, and 35 of them have a usable scan. The
tumours in breasts with a usable scan have a median biopsy size of 10\.0 mm, against
9\.0 mm in the others.

The biopsy size is not the size of the tumour: it is the length of tumour seen along a needle core, which is only 1-2 cm long, so it can never be
larger than the core. The imaging reports measure the mass itself. In the 57 breasts with both, the imaging size is larger in
**54**, with a median of **19 mm** against
9 mm from the biopsy. The imaging sizes are taken from the report text and can include more than one
mass in a breast, so they are approximate.

::: {.callout-important title="We do not need to hit the tumour precisely"}
Even when the operator is guided by the mammogram or ultrasound (a quadrant, a clock position and a distance from the nipple), the beam can only
be placed approximately: the breast is positioned differently on our instrument than on the mammogram, and the tumours are small, typically about
2 cm across on imaging. It is unlikely that our beams pass through the middle of the tumour,
and for many breasts they will miss it altogether. Yet the CANCER breast still comes out wetter in most CANCER/NORMAL patients, and the tumour size
makes little difference to which breasts give a usable scan. The signal does not depend on going through the tumour: scanning the glandular tissue
**near** it, or in the same breast, is enough. **High positioning accuracy is not needed**; what matters is that each scan reaches glandular
tissue (@sec-on-the-fly).
:::
